column4: The section contrasts a shared, straight road with people scattering in every direction; the command says “هَٰذَا صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا فَاتَّبِعُوهُ” and warns that following “السُّبُلَ” divides people from His way. The many paths make the communal, already trodden route a practical choice of what to follow.

The section’s “dāllīn” are those who fail to find the way and its middle; this verse says “ضَلَّ سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ” of someone who has lost the middle of the way. It makes the image of losing the road’s center explicit in Quranic wording.

As Moses heads toward Midian, he hopes “أَن يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ.” The phrase “middle of the way” directly clarifies the section’s dictionary image of keeping to the road’s middle while travelling.

The section pictures a traveller finding the route and its destination; here God places mountains, rivers, and “سُبُلًا” in the earth “لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ.” Paths are part of the created landscape by which travellers can find their way.

The section’s “worlds” carries the dictionary echo of a landmark, and this verse names “عَلَامَاتٍ” and says people find their way by the stars. It joins markers and guidance in the very scene the image evokes.

The section describes one who cannot find the road or home; this verse depicts a person “حَيْرَانَ” on earth, while companions call him “إِلَى الْهُدَى ائْتِنَا.” The lost traveller and those calling him back make the contrast between disorientation and a guided community concrete.

The section’s road is a route someone must keep following; Iblis swears “لَأَقْعُدَنَّ لَهُمْ صِرَاطَكَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ,” placing an adversary directly on it. This shows that a clear road can still be obstructed.

After 7:16 places Iblis on the straight path, this verse names the approaches “مِن بَيْنِ أَيْدِيهِمْ” and “مِنْ خَلْفِهِمْ” and from right and left. The linked verse completes the ambush scene by showing pressure from around the route.

The section’s scattered people go every way, while this command forbids sitting “بِكُلِّ صِرَاطٍ” to threaten people and turn them from Allah’s way. It gives the image a social counterpart: a route can be blocked and its travellers diverted.

The section says guidance shows both the road and the home it reaches; here God calls to “دَارِ السَّلَامِ” and guides whom He wills “إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” The destination named beside the path fills out where the guided journey leads.

Abraham tells his father “فَاتَّبِعْنِي أَهْدِكَ صِرَاطًا سَوِيًّا.” A guide walks ahead and invites another to follow, closely matching the section’s account of hidaya as showing a route and leading along it.

The believing man in Pharaoh’s household says “اتَّبِعُونِ أَهْدِكُمْ سَبِيلَ الرَّشَادِ.” His invitation to follow him along the way of right guidance gives the section’s leading guide a speaker and a concrete communal setting.

The verse asks who is better guided: one who walks “مُكِبًّا عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ” or one who walks upright “سَوِيًّا عَلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” Its bodily contrast makes the section’s straight, walkable route perceptible as a way of moving, not only a correctness claim.

In the context of the Book clarifying God’s pleasure, the verse says God guides followers to “سُبُلَ السَّلَامِ,” brings them from darkness to light, and guides them “إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” It connects following, multiple routes of peace, and arrival at a straight way.
The verse says God made the earth a resting place and made “سُبُلًا” in it “لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ.” This grounds the section’s road and guidance in the earth’s traversable landscape.

The section asks for guidance along the way of those granted favor; here the command is “فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ.” The same guiding and path language leads to the opposite destination, exposing guidance as inseparable from where a route ends.

God says to the Prophet “وَوَجَدَكَ ضَالًّا فَهَدَىٰ.” The section’s lost traveller and its contrast between ضلّ and هدى illuminate this statement while leaving its possible senses of searching or being without guidance open.

The verse says “إِنَّا هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيلَ” and then names gratitude or ingratitude as the response. It parallels the section’s road with a way shown to a traveller whose subsequent direction is not automatic.

The Prophet is told to say “هَدَانِي رَبِّي إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ” and to name it “دِينًا قِيَمًا.” The verse brings guidance, a straight route, and an upright way of life together, as the section’s root echoes suggest.
Jesus says “فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.” The verse explicitly places worship on the straight path, making audible the section’s adjacent roots for “we worship” and “straight.”

Jesus says “إِنَّ اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبُّكُمْ فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.” Like the section’s sequence from worship to the request for a path, this verse names worship itself as that path.

Jesus says “فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.” This second Quranic formulation, in a passage affirming God as Lord, makes the section’s root echo between worship and the straight road explicit.

The address to Adam’s children says “وَأَنِ اعْبُدُونِي هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.” The shared formulation directly joins worship to the straight route, as the section’s movement from “نَعْبُدُ” to “الصِّرَاطَ” does.

Immediately after identifying worship as a straight path in 36:61, the verse says Satan “أَضَلَّ مِنكُمْ جِبِلًّا كَثِيرًا.” It supplies the section’s contrary image of many people led away from the road.
The verse tells the Prophet “وَإِنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” It gives the section’s guide who walks ahead a Quranic instance: the Messenger leads people toward the straight route.
In a passage about obeying God and the Messenger, the verse promises “وَلَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا.” This directly joins obedience to being guided onto a straight route.

The verse says God will admit believers to mercy and grace and “يَهْدِيهِمْ إِلَيْهِ صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا.” It makes the section’s destination-bearing sense of hidaya explicit: the route leads “to Him.”

The verse says whoever holds fast to God “فَقَدْ هُدِيَ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” That image of holding fast alongside being guided makes the route something one remains attached to, echoing the section’s continued walking without leaving the way.

After describing the person God guides as having an opened breast and the one left astray as constricted, the verse says “هَٰذَا صِرَاطُ رَبِّكَ مُسْتَقِيمًا.” It links the section’s straight route with the contrasting states of those able or unable to receive guidance.

After speaking of those given knowledge recognizing the revelation as truth, the verse says “وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَهَادِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” It presents belief as a community led onto the route the section asks to follow.

The verse says “وَعَلَى اللَّهِ قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ” and that some ways are “جَائِرٌ.” Its distinction between the directed way and crooked routes gives the section’s straight path a clear boundary against deviation.

The parable contrasts a dependent person unable to accomplish anything with one who “يَأْمُرُ بِالْعَدْلِ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” It makes the straight-path figure an active, upright agent, adding force to the section’s embodied image of walking rather than merely knowing.

The verse says “وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ,” that God showed the human being two conspicuous ways. It supplies a concrete fork in the route that sharpens the section’s contrast between walking the favored way and losing it.

The verse promises believers a light “تَمْشُونَ بِهِ” (by which you walk). This image of walking by granted light parallels the section’s route and its landmarks, while making the aid visible along the journey.

The verse warns the People of the Book not to follow a people who “ضَلُّوا عَن سَوَاءِ السَّبِيلِ.” Its context links deviation to following others’ desires, sharpening the section’s contrast between the favored community’s route and those who have left it.

The verse says God made the stars so people may “لِتَهْتَدُوا بِهَا” in the darkness of land and sea. This gives the section’s route markers a concrete counterpart: heavenly signs help a traveller keep direction when the way is hard to see.

The verse says the arrogant turn from signs, do not take “سَبِيلَ الرُّشْدِ” when they see it, and take “سَبِيلَ الْغَيِّ” instead. Its opposition between visible routes explains how a person can see markers and still choose the way that leads astray.

After the account of Adam, God says “فَمَنِ اتَّبَعَ هُدَايَ فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ.” It directly links following revealed guidance with not losing the way, the outcome sought by the section’s prayer.

The Prophet is told “فَاسْتَمْسِكْ بِالَّذِي أُوحِيَ إِلَيْكَ إِنَّكَ عَلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” Holding fast to revelation while already on the straight path matches the section’s account of continuing without turning aside.

On Judgment Day the wrongdoer regrets “يَا لَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا.” His wish to have taken a way with the Messenger makes the section’s path of a guided community painfully concrete: the route depended on whom he chose to follow.

The next verse names the prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous as good company for those who obey God and the Messenger. It completes 4:68 by showing a community of exemplars walking the straight route the section calls the path of those granted favor.

The section distinguishes the path of those granted favor from those who stray; this address tells the criminals “وَامْتَازُوا الْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا الْمُجْرِمُونَ.” In the same passage, 36:61 names worship as the straight path, so the separation marks the boundary around that call.

The next verse calls it “صِرَاطِ اللَّهِ” and says to Him belongs what is in the heavens and earth and all affairs return. It completes 42:52 by naming whose route it is and the destination to which it returns.

Amid objections to the change of prayer direction, the verse says “يَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” The disputed direction makes the straight path a divinely set orientation, rather than a route established by every onlooker’s judgment.

After describing people as one community who then differed, the verse says God guided believers to the truth in their disputes and “يَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” This sets the section’s shared road against divisions that leave people without a common way.

In a passage comparing people who are deaf and dumb in darkness with those God wills to guide, the verse says He may place a person “عَلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” It connects the section’s lost way and guided way to the contrast between disorientation and a clear route.

After naming prophets and their forefathers, the verse says “وَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” The guided predecessors give the section’s “path of those You favored” named exemplars who have already been led along it.

After saying God has sent clear signs, the verse says “وَاللَّهُ يَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” The signs and guidance together echo the section’s route and its landmarks, while the verse makes clear that guidance is granted by God.

The verse promises “لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا” to those who strive for God and says God is with the doers of good. Its plural “ways” ties continued effort to being led, complementing the section’s road as a practice walked over time.

In the warning against obeying parents who press toward associating partners with God, the verse still says “وَاتَّبِعْ سَبِيلَ مَنْ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّ.” It gives a concrete model to follow along a path, matching the section’s communal route while marking a contrary direction.

The verse says God made leaders “يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا” when they were patient and certain of His signs. It supplies the section’s guide who goes ahead with a community, grounded in patience and recognized signs.

The jinn describe the revelation as confirming Moses’ scripture and “يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ وَإِلَىٰ طَرِيقٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.” Their report gives the straight way a revealed guide and shows others recognizing that route.

The verse says God forgives the Prophet and “يَهْدِيَكَ صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا.” It frames the Messenger himself as guided along a straight route, complementing the section’s sense of a guide who has a way to lead others on.

The Quran is a reminder “لِمَن شَاءَ مِنكُمْ أَن يَسْتَقِيمَ,” followed by the reminder that human willing depends on God’s will. The shared root of “المستقيم” connects straightness to keeping one’s course, while the context preserves God’s authority over that course.

The regret in 25:27 is explained when the speaker says “لَقَدْ أَضَلَّنِي عَنِ الذِّكْرِ بَعْدَ إِذْ جَاءَنِي.” This neighbor identifies the companion who led him away from the route he wishes he had taken with the Messenger.

The Prophet is commanded to say “أَدْعُو إِلَى اللَّهِ عَلَىٰ بَصِيرَةٍ أَنَا وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَنِي.” It pairs a caller who sees clearly with people who follow him, echoing the section’s guide and the community walking behind him.

The verse says “وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ,” naming a guide for every people. It gives the section’s “hādī” a communal setting: guidance is associated with someone who leads a people, not only private direction.

The messengers say God has “هَدَانَا سُبُلَنَا” and that they will endure the harm done to them. It connects being shown a route with remaining on it through opposition, a pressure implied by the section’s insistence on continuing without deviation.

The Prophet is commanded “فَاسْتَقِمْ كَمَا أُمِرْتَ” and not to follow others’ desires after knowledge has come. The same root as “المستقيم” makes straightness an ongoing stance of not leaving the course.
